content: 1. When using a spacer device, allow the child to breathe normally for three to five breaths. This process can be repeated in quick succession until the child has received six puffs of the medication if they are under five years old, or twelve puffs if they are older than five years. After administering the appropriate number of puffs, assess the child’s response and repeat the treatment as needed until their condition improves. In severe cases, six or twelve puffs may be given multiple times within an hour for a short duration. 2. Some infants and young children may respond better to treatment when a face mask is attached to the spacer instead of a mouthpiece. If commercial spacer devices are unavailable, a spacer can be improvised using a plastic cup or a 1-liter plastic bottle. These devices can deliver three to four puffs of salbutamol, and the child should breathe from the device for up to 30 seconds. 3. If there is no improvement after 15 minutes, the dose of salbutamol can be repeated once. For severe or life-threatening acute wheezing episodes, oral prednisolone should be administered at a dose of 1 mg/kg for three to five days, with a maximum dose of 60 mg. For children aged 2–5 years, a dose of 20 mg is recommended. If the child remains critically ill, continue treatment until improvement is observed. If the child vomits, repeat the dose of prednisolone, and consider intravenous steroids if oral medication cannot be retained. 4. Short courses of steroids (7–14 days) do not require tapering. Intravenous hydrocortisone (4 mg/kg every 4 hours) does not provide additional benefit and should only be used in children unable to retain oral medication. Intravenous magnesium sulfate may offer additional benefit in children with severe asthma who are already being treated with bronchodilators and corticosteroids. Magnesium sulfate has a favorable safety profile in managing acute severe asthma. 5. Aminophylline is not recommended for children with mild-to-moderate acute asthma. It is reserved for children who do not improve after several doses of a rapid-acting bronchodilator combined with oral prednisolone. If aminophylline is indicated, the child should ideally be admitted to a high-care or intensive-care unit for continuous monitoring. Administer an initial loading dose of 5–6 mg/kg (up to a maximum of 300 mg) intravenously over at least 20 minutes, preferably over one hour, followed by a maintenance dose of 5 mg/kg every six hours. Avoid the initial dose if the child has received aminophylline or caffeine in the previous 24 hours. Discontinue immediately if the child develops vomiting, a pulse rate exceeding 180 beats per minute, headache, or convulsions. 6. Oral salbutamol (in syrup or tablet form) is not recommended for treating severe or persistent wheezing. It should only be used when inhaled salbutamol is unavailable and the child has improved sufficiently to be discharged home. Dosage for oral salbutamol is as follows: for children aged 1 month to 2 years, 100 µg/kg (maximum 2 mg) up to four times daily; for children aged 2–6 years, 1–2 mg up to four times daily. 7. Antibiotics should not be routinely prescribed for asthma or for children with asthma who exhibit fast breathing without fever. Supportive care should include ensuring the child receives daily maintenance fluids appropriate for their age, encouraging breastfeeding and oral fluids, and promoting adequate complementary feeding as soon as the child can tolerate food. 8. Monitor the child’s respiratory status closely, recording respiratory rate and observing for signs of respiratory failure, such as increasing hypoxia and respiratory distress leading to exhaustion. Oxygen therapy should be monitored as described in clinical guidelines. If the child fails to respond to therapy or their condition worsens suddenly, obtain a chest X-ray to check for pneumothorax. Be cautious in interpreting the X-ray, as hyperinflation in asthma can mimic pneumothorax. 9. For long-term management, once the child has improved sufficiently to be discharged home, prescribe inhaled salbutamol via a metered-dose inhaler with a suitable spacer. Educate the caregiver on its proper use. Develop a long-term treatment plan based on the frequency and severity of symptoms, which may include intermittent or regular bronchodilator use, regular inhaled steroids, or intermittent courses of oral steroids. Consult up-to-date international or specialized national guidelines for further information. 10. Stridor, a harsh noise during inspiration, is caused by narrowing of the air passages in the oropharynx, subglottis, or trachea. If the obstruction is below the larynx, stridor may also occur during expiration. Severe stridor can result from viral croup, foreign body inhalation, retropharyngeal abscess, diphtheria, or trauma to the larynx. It may also occur in early infancy due to congenital abnormalities. 11. Viral croup, which causes upper airway obstruction, is most severe in children aged ≤2 years. Mild croup is characterized by fever, a hoarse voice, a barking or hacking cough, and stridor heard only when the child is agitated. Severe croup includes stridor at rest, rapid breathing, lower chest indrawing, and cyanosis or oxygen saturation ≤90%. Children with severe croup should be admitted to the hospital. 12. Avoid invasive procedures unless performed in the presence of an anesthetist, as they may precipitate complete airway obstruction. Administer steroids as soon as possible, such as dexamethasone or prednisolone, or nebulized budesonide if available. Dissolve tablets in water for children unable to swallow them. Repeat the dose if the child vomits. 13. Nebulized adrenaline (2 ml of 1:1000 solution) can be trialed and repeated hourly if effective, with careful monitoring. While this treatment may provide temporary improvement within 30 minutes, its effects often last only about two hours. Antibiotics are not effective and should not be given. 14. Monitor the child closely and ensure facilities for emergency intubation or tracheostomy are immediately available, as airway obstruction can occur suddenly. If signs of impending complete airway obstruction are present, such as severe lower chest wall indrawing and restlessness, intubate the child immediately. If intubation is not possible, transfer the child urgently to a hospital where emergency tracheostomy can be performed by experienced staff. 15. Avoid using oxygen unless there is impending airway obstruction. Signs such as severe lower chest wall indrawing and restlessness are more indicative of the need for intubation or tracheostomy than oxygen. Nasal prongs or nasopharyngeal catheters can upset the child and precipitate airway obstruction. However, oxygen should be administered if intubation or tracheostomy is deemed necessary. 16. Keep the child calm and avoid unnecessary disturbances. If the child has difficulty swallowing, nasogastric feeding may be required, and the tube should be placed by an experienced clinician or anesthetist. Avoid frequent examinations and invasive procedures unless absolutely necessary. 17. Diphtheria, a bacterial infection preventable by immunization, can cause a grey membrane in the upper airway or nasopharynx, leading to stridor and obstruction. Nasal involvement produces a bloody discharge. Diphtheria toxin can cause muscular paralysis and myocarditis, which are associated with mortality. Administer 40,000 U of diphtheria antitoxin (IM or IV) immediately, as delays increase mortality risk. Perform an intradermal test for hypersensitivity to the antitoxin and have treatment for anaphylaxis available. 18. Myocarditis and paralysis may occur 2–7 weeks after the onset of diphtheria. Signs of myocarditis include a weak, irregular pulse and evidence of heart failure. Refer to standard pediatric textbooks for detailed diagnosis and management of myocarditis. 19. For public health measures, nurse the child in a separate room with staff fully vaccinated against diphtheria. Vaccinated household contacts should receive a diphtheria toxoid booster. Unvaccinated contacts should receive one dose of benzathine penicillin and diphtheria toxoid, and be monitored daily for five days for signs of diphtheria. 20. Epiglottitis, a medical emergency, is primarily caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b but may also result from other bacteria or viruses. It begins as inflammation and swelling between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis, potentially obstructing the airway. Symptoms include sore throat, difficulty speaking, breathing difficulty, soft stridor, fever, drooling, and difficulty swallowing.
